name: findymail-mcp

tools.name: find_email
tools.description: Find a verified B2B email address for one person. Identify them either by full name plus company domain, or by LinkedIn profile URL — one of those two combinations is required, and the LinkedIn URL takes precedence when both are supplied. Returns the contact with the email address, the person's name and the company domain. Addresses are verified before being returned, so a person whose address cannot be verified comes back as not found rather than as a guess. Use it when you need one specific person's email, and chain it after `find_employees` (passing the returned name + domain, or the returned LinkedIn URL) to put emails on a list of contacts. Set list_id to also save the contact found into one of your contact lists (see `list_contact_lists`). Costs 1 finder credit per email found; a lookup that finds nothing is not charged.

list_id.description: Contact list to save the contact found into, from `list_contact_lists` or `create_contact_list`. Omit to save it to your contacts only.

tools.name: find_employees
tools.description: Find employees at a company by job title. Given a company website or domain and a list of target job titles, returns matching contacts with name, job title, company and LinkedIn URL. Email addresses are not part of the response: to get a verified email for a contact, pass the returned name and domain — or the returned LinkedIn URL — to `find_email`. Use it to build a shortlist of people to reach at a known company; to discover the companies themselves, use `generate_lead_list` or `lookalike_search` first. Costs 1 finder credit per contact returned.

job_titles.description: Target job titles (max 10, each max 50 characters, e.g., ["CTO", "VP Engineering"])

count.description: Number of contacts to return (min: 1, max: 5, default: 1)

tools.name: find_phone
tools.description: Find the phone number(s) of a contact, identified by their LinkedIn profile URL. Use it once you already have a LinkedIn URL for the person — returned by `find_employees` or `reverse_email_lookup`, or supplied by the user — and need to reach them by phone; a phone number cannot be looked up from a name or an email address. Returns the contact with the mobile and direct-dial numbers found, or an empty result when no number is available. Costs 10 finder credits per phone number found; a lookup that finds nothing is not charged.

tools.name: verify_email
tools.description: Check whether an email address is deliverable, without sending anything to it. Use it on addresses that came from elsewhere (a CRM export, a spreadsheet, the user) before adding them to an outreach sequence. Addresses returned by `find_email` and `generate_lead_list` are already verified and do not need a second pass. Costs 1 verifier credit per address checked — verifier credits are a separate pool from the finder credits the lookup tools spend.

tools.name: enrich_company
tools.description: Look up firmographic data for one company. Identify it by domain, by LinkedIn company page URL, or by name — at least one is required, and the domain is used first when several are given, since company names are ambiguous. Returns the company profile: name, domain, description, industry, employee-count range, location and social profiles. Use it to qualify a single company before prospecting it, or to fill in a company whose domain came out of `find_employees` or `reverse_email_lookup`. To find many companies at once, use `lookalike_search` or `generate_lead_list` instead. Costs 1 finder credit per company returned.

tools.name: reverse_email_lookup
tools.description: Identify the person behind an email address. Returns their LinkedIn profile URL; set with_profile to also return the full LinkedIn profile (name, job title, company etc.). Use it to put a name and a company on an address that arrived without context — an inbound reply, a CRM row, an imported list — and chain the returned LinkedIn URL into `find_phone` when you need to reach them by phone. It says nothing about deliverability: use `verify_email` for that. Costs 1 finder credit per contact found, or 2 finder credits when with_profile returns complete profile data; an address that matches nobody is not charged.

tools.name: lookalike_search
tools.description: Find companies similar to a given seed company. Given a company domain (e.g. "stripe.com"), returns a list of lookalike companies that share similar business characteristics using semantic similarity. Results can be filtered by same country and/or same company size. Exclusion lists can be provided to remove already-known companies from results. Costs 1 finder credit per 10 results returned.

seed.description: The domain or URL of the seed company to find lookalikes for (e.g. "stripe.com" or "https://www.stripe.com/pricing"). URLs are automatically resolved to their root domain.

same_country.description: When true, only return companies located in the same country as the seed company

same_size.description: When true, only return companies with a similar employee count range as the seed company

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (min: 1, max: 10,000)

exclusion_list_ids.description: IDs of exclusion lists whose domains should be removed from results. Unlike `generate_lead_list`, this parameter does NOT accept the [0] / [-1] markers — pass real list IDs only (from `list_exclusion_lists`), or leave it empty for no filtering.

tools.name: generate_lead_list
tools.description: Start a company discovery run from a natural language description of an ideal customer profile. This is a semantic search, not a database lookup, so describe the kind of company you are looking for rather than listing exact filter values (e.g. "SaaS companies in the USA with 50+ employees", "tech startups offering insurance services in NYC"). Use 'targeted' mode to return only companies strictly matching the description (narrower) or `broad` mode to return companies loosely matching the description (broader). Matching companies can be enriched with contacts, verified email addresses and phone numbers. The run is asynchronous and this call returns only a hash: pass that hash to `get_lead_list_results` to follow progress and retrieve the results. Credit cost depends on the options chosen — 1 finder credit per 10 companies in 'broad' mode or 1 per company in 'targeted' mode, plus 1 per contact found, 1 per email found and 10 per phone number found.

query.description: Natural language description of what you're looking for (max 1000 characters)

mode.description: 'broad' = fast export (1 credit/10 companies), 'targeted' = AI-qualified results (1 credit/company)

find_contact.description: Search for contacts at each company (+1 credit/contact found)

target_job_titles.description: Job titles to target when find_contact is true. Either one flat list, where every title has the same priority (e.g. ['CEO', 'CTO']), or up to 3 priority tiers, each a non-empty list: the contact is searched with the first tier and the next tier is only tried at companies where nothing matched (e.g. [['CTO'], ['VP Engineering', 'Head of Engineering'], ['CEO']]). Never mix the two shapes in one list.

find_email.description: Enrich contacts with email (+1 credit/email found). Requires find_contact: true

find_phone.description: Enrich contacts with phone (+10 credits/phone found). Requires find_contact: true

exclusion_list_ids.description: IDs of exclusion lists whose domains must be filtered out of the results. Omit this parameter to keep the default behaviour. [0] means "every exclusion source you can reach" (your global exclusions plus every list you own or share) — NOT just the global one. [-1] disables exclusion filtering entirely, and so does an empty array. Never mix these markers with real list IDs: [0, 12] silently ignores 12 and filters on everything, and [-1, 12] silently disables filtering altogether. Pass either exactly [0], exactly [-1], or real list IDs — never a mixture. Get them from `list_exclusion_lists`.

save_to_list_id.description: Contact list to save every contact found into, from `list_contact_lists` or `create_contact_list`. Omit to save them to your contacts only. Only contacts with an email address can be read back from a list (`list_contacts`, and the web app alike), so with find_email false the list looks empty even when contacts were found.

add_to_exclusion_list_id.description: ID of an exclusion list to automatically add every exported company domain to, so later searches never return them again. The domains are written once, at the very end of the export: nothing is added if the export fails, and if that final write itself fails the export is still reported as successful — check with `list_exclusion_domains` when it matters. Only pass an ID returned by `list_exclusion_lists`, or create one with `create_exclusion_list`.

tools.name: get_lead_list_results
tools.description: Follow a lead list run started with `generate_lead_list` and read its results one page at a time. Takes the hash returned by `generate_lead_list`. By default it waits for the run for up to 50 seconds; set wait to false for a single status check that answers at once. While the run is going, returns status "processing" with its progress — call again to keep waiting. Once it is done, returns status "success" with one page of results under `data`, plus `page`, `last_page` and `total` (the number of rows in the whole run): pass page + 1 to read the next one while `has_more` is true. Only ask for the pages you need — a 5,000-row run is 50 pages at the default size, and each page lands in your context. Consumes no credits, whatever the number of pages read: the run itself was charged by `generate_lead_list`.

page.description: Page of results to return once the run is done (default: 1)

wait.description: Wait up to 50s for the run to finish (default), or false to check its status once and answer at once

tools.name: get_credit_balance
tools.description: Return the credits left on your account. Call it before starting a run that can spend many credits — a large `generate_lead_list`, or a loop of finder calls over hundreds of rows — so you can compare the estimated cost with what is left and ask the user before going ahead. Returns `credits` (finder credits left, used by every lookup tool and by lead lists), `verifier_credits` (credits left for `verify_email` — absent when the account is on unified pricing, where a single `credits` pool pays for everything) and `has_capacity`. Read them by plan: when `has_capacity` is null, the account buys credits and `credits` is exactly what it can spend. When `has_capacity` is true or false, the account is on a usage-capacity plan: spending first draws on rolling usage windows that refill over time, and `credits` is only an extra balance on top, often 0 — so `credits: 0` with `has_capacity: true` does not mean the run will be refused. `has_capacity` false means nothing is left right now; calls are refused until the windows refill. On a team, the balance and the capacity are the team owner's, shared by every member. Consumes no credits.

tools.name: get_credit_usage
tools.description: Report how many finder and verifier credits were spent over a date range. By default it covers your own usage, broken down by day — or by month when the range is longer than 2 months — under `items`, with the totals under `total`. Set team to true for a per-member summary of the whole team under `members`; only the team owner may do that, anyone else gets a 403. Use it to explain where credits went or to compare spend with what is left (`get_credit_balance`). On a usage-capacity plan (`has_capacity` not null in `get_credit_balance`), spend absorbed by the usage windows may not show here. Consumes no credits.

from.description: First day of the report, included (YYYY-MM-DD). Defaults to 30 days ago.

to.description: Last day of the report, included (YYYY-MM-DD). Defaults to today.

team.description: Summarize every team member instead of your own usage. Team owner only.

tools.name: list_exclusion_lists
tools.description: List the exclusion lists you can use (lists you own plus lists shared with your team). An exclusion list holds company domains that should never show up in search results. Returns each list's id, name, owner and sharing status — use those ids with `generate_lead_list` (exclusion_list_ids / add_to_exclusion_list_id), with `lookalike_search`, or with the other exclusion tools. Consumes no credits.

tools.name: create_exclusion_list
tools.description: Create a new, empty exclusion list and return its id. Add domains to it with `add_exclusion_domains`, or let a search fill it automatically via `generate_lead_list`'s add_to_exclusion_list_id. List names must be unique per user. If is_shared is true and you do not belong to a team, the list is still created but the call returns an error — do not retry with the same name, it would then fail as a duplicate. Call `list_exclusion_lists` to check before retrying. Consumes no credits.

name.description: Name of the list (max 255 characters, must be unique among your lists, e.g. "Competitors")

is_shared.description: Share the list with your current team. Fails if you do not belong to a team.

tools.name: list_exclusion_domains
tools.description: List the domains held by an exclusion list, paginated. Each domain is returned with its own id — those ids are what `remove_exclusion_domains` needs, so call this first when you want to remove domains. Omitting list_id does NOT return only your global exclusions: it returns EVERY domain you can reach — your global ones, every list you own, AND every list shared with your team. To act on the global exclusions only, keep the entries whose `excluded_domain_list_id` is null. Always pass an explicit list_id before deleting anything. Results are ordered by domain name alone, so an entry can move between pages — re-read the page before using an id. Consumes no credits.

list_id.description: Exclusion list to read. Must be >= 1 — 0 is refused. Omit the parameter to list every domain you can reach (see the tool description). Get ids from `list_exclusion_lists`.

query.description: Filter domains containing this text (max 100 characters, e.g. "competitor")

tools.name: add_exclusion_domains
tools.description: Add company domains to an exclusion list so they stop appearing in search results. Omit list_id to add them to your global exclusions instead. Domains are reduced to their registrable form before storage: protocol, path and ALL subdomains are stripped, so "careers.acme.com" and "https://www.acme.com/jobs" both become "acme.com" and exclude the whole company. Entries that cannot be parsed as a domain are dropped silently and are not reported back. The response counters do NOT reflect what was stored: `total` and `processed_immediately` count the entries you sent, dropped ones included, so `total: 4` can mean 3 domains excluded — read the list back with `list_exclusion_domains` to know what landed. Large batches are accepted (max 10,000): the first 50 domains are applied immediately and the rest are queued in the background, so a search started right away will only account for the first 50. Consumes no credits.

domains.description: Company domains to exclude (max 10,000, each max 255 characters, e.g. ["competitor.com", "blocked.io"])

list_id.description: Exclusion list to add the domains to. Omit to add them as global exclusions — 0 does the same here, unlike `list_exclusion_domains` where 0 is refused. Get ids from `list_exclusion_lists`.

tools.name: remove_exclusion_domains
tools.description: Remove domains from an exclusion list, making them eligible for search results again. Takes domain ids, NOT domain names — call `list_exclusion_domains` first to resolve names into ids. Deletion is permanent: there is no undo and no soft delete. If none of the ids are yours to delete the call fails with a 403 rather than reporting a count of zero; if only some are, the others are dropped silently and the response does not say which. On a team-shared list you are allowed to delete domains added by teammates, so check the list before deleting. Ids obtained right after a large `add_exclusion_domains` may be stale. Consumes no credits.

ids.description: Ids of the domains to remove (max 1000), as returned by `list_exclusion_domains`

tools.name: search_technologies
tools.description: Search the Findymail technology catalog by name and return up to 25 matches, each with its exact name, category and subcategory. Use it to check that a technology is known, and how it is spelled, before naming it in a `generate_lead_list` query ("companies using HubSpot") or filtering `get_company_technologies` on it. Rate-limited to 10 calls per minute. Consumes no credits.

query.description: Technology name or part of it (min 2 characters, e.g. "hubspot")

tools.name: get_company_technologies
tools.description: Return the technology stack detected for one company, identified by its domain: each technology with its name, category, subcategory and when it was last detected. Set technologies to only check for specific ones (case-insensitive names, e.g. ["Salesforce", "HubSpot"]) — an empty `technologies` array in the response then means none of them was detected. A large company can run hundreds of technologies, so at most limit of them are returned (default 50); `total` gives the full count and `truncated` is true when some were left out — narrow with technologies or categories rather than raising limit. Use it to qualify an account on its stack before prospecting it. Costs 1 finder credit when the company has at least one technology matching technologies (whatever categories and limit leave out of the response); an empty result is not charged.

technologies.description: Only return these technologies, matched by name, case-insensitively (max 50). Check exact names with `search_technologies`.

categories.description: Only return technologies in these categories, as `search_technologies` spells them (e.g. ["sales", "marketing"])

limit.description: Maximum number of technologies to return (default: 50, max: 500)

tools.name: list_contact_lists
tools.description: List the contact lists you can use: the ones you own plus the ones shared with your team. A contact list holds people you found and saved — not to be confused with exclusion lists, which hold company domains to keep out of searches. Returns each list's id, name, whether it is shared with your team and whether you own it. Use the ids with `list_contacts`, `find_email` and `generate_lead_list` (to save what they find into a list), `create_monitor` (lead_list_id) and the other contact list tools. Consumes no credits.

tools.name: create_contact_list
tools.description: Create a new, empty contact list and return it with its id. Fill it by passing that id to `find_email` (list_id) or `generate_lead_list` (save_to_list_id), or as lead_list_id to a monitor (`create_monitor`). Names are not unique: calling this twice creates two lists with the same name, so check `list_contact_lists` first. The list is private; share it with `update_contact_list`. Consumes no credits.

tools.name: update_contact_list
tools.description: Rename a contact list, or share it with your team or stop sharing it. Pass only what changes: whatever you omit keeps its current value. Only lists you may edit can be changed; anything else fails with a 403. Consumes no credits.

shared.description: true to share the list with your current team, false to stop sharing it

tools.name: delete_contact_list
tools.description: Delete a contact list. This is irreversible: the list and its grouping of contacts are gone for good, for you and for every teammate it was shared with, and there is no undo. The contacts themselves are not deleted — they stay in your saved contacts (`list_contacts` with list_id 0). Confirm with the user before calling it. Consumes no credits.

tools.name: list_contacts
tools.description: Read back contacts you saved, one page at a time: from one contact list, or from all your saved contacts with list_id 0. Each contact comes with its id, name, email, LinkedIn URL, company and job title; only contacts with an email address are returned. Page with offset and limit, and keep going while `has_more` is true. The API gives no total count and no guaranteed order, so a contact saved while you page may shift the pages. Consumes no credits.

list_id.description: Contact list to read, from `list_contact_lists`. 0 (default) reads all your saved contacts.

tools.name: list_signals
tools.description: List the buying signals your monitors detected (yours and your team's shared ones), most recent first, one page at a time. Each signal comes with its type, the matching contact and company, what triggered it (keyword, post, new job…) and the monitors that caught it, with their AI relevance score when one is configured. Filter by type, monitor, detection date or relevance score. Read a single signal with `get_signal`, and manage what is watched with the monitor tools. Consumes no credits: signals are charged when a monitor delivers them.

monitor_id.description: Only signals caught by this monitor, from `list_monitors`

date_from.description: Only signals detected on or after this day (YYYY-MM-DD)

date_to.description: Only signals detected on or before this day (YYYY-MM-DD)

relevance_scores.description: Only signals whose AI relevance score is one of these (0-5, e.g. [4, 5]). Scores exist only on monitors with an ai_relevance_prompt; combine with monitor_id to score against one monitor.

ownership.description: Only signals from your own monitors (my), your teammates' shared ones (team), or both (all, default)

tools.name: get_signal
tools.description: Read one signal by id, as returned by `list_signals`: its type, what triggered it, the matching contact and company, and which of your monitors caught it. Signals you have no access to fail with a 403. Consumes no credits.

tools.name: list_monitors
tools.description: List the signal monitors you can see — yours and the ones teammates shared — most recent first. A monitor watches LinkedIn and job boards for one kind of buying signal and delivers each match as a signal. Returns each monitor's id, name, type, status (active or paused), filters, enrichment level, contact list, match cap and match_count. Use the ids with `list_signals`, `update_monitor` and `delete_monitor`. Consumes no credits.

ownership.description: Only your own monitors (my), your teammates' shared ones (team), or both (all, default)

tools.name: create_monitor
tools.description: Create a signal monitor that keeps running in the background and delivers every match as a signal (read them with `list_signals`). Types: "keyword_mention" (LinkedIn posts mentioning keywords — keywords required), "post_engagement" (people who like or comment a LinkedIn post or profile's posts — engagement_types plus post_url, profile_url or keywords), "new_hire" and "job_change" (people starting a new job — target_companies or icp_filters required), "company_hiring" (companies posting job offers — job_offer_title_keywords required, enrichment_level must be "none"). The API answers a 422 naming any missing or forbidden field for the type. COST: every signal delivered charges finder credits for as long as the monitor runs — 1 credit per signal for new_hire, job_change and company_hiring; for keyword_mention and post_engagement, 1 plus 1 with company-level icp_filters (industries, sizes, countries) and 1 more with contact-level ones (job titles, seniority), so up to 3. Set max_matches to cap the total spend: the monitor pauses itself once it is reached. Plans limit how many monitors can be active at once. Get the user's go-ahead on the type, filters and match cap before creating one.

signal_type.description: Kind of signal to watch for (cannot be changed later)

keywords.description: Keywords to watch for (max 5, each max 100 characters). Required for keyword_mention, and for post_engagement without post_url or profile_url.

engagement_types.description: post_engagement only (required there): which engagements to catch

target_companies.description: new_hire and job_change only: company names or domains to watch (max 100). Without it, icp_filters is required.

job_offer_title_keywords.description: company_hiring only (required there): job offer title keywords, substring match, any of them (max 10)

industries.description: LinkedIn industry names (Industry Codes V2), e.g. ["Biotechnology"]

job_title_keywords.description: Contact job title keywords (max 10). Not for company_hiring.

icp_filters.description: Narrow the matches to an ideal customer profile. Company-level filters (industries, sizes, countries) and contact-level ones (job titles, seniority) each add 1 credit per signal on keyword_mention and post_engagement.

enrichment_level.description: What to look up for each matched contact. Must be "none" for company_hiring.

lead_list_id.description: Contact list to save every matched contact into, from `list_contact_lists`

webhook_url.description: HTTPS URL to notify on each new signal

ai_relevance_prompt.description: What makes a signal relevant to the user (max 500 characters); each signal then gets a 0-5 relevance score

is_shared.description: Share the monitor with your current team

post_url.description: post_engagement only: HTTPS URL of the LinkedIn post to watch. Not with profile_url.

profile_url.description: post_engagement only: HTTPS URL of the LinkedIn profile whose posts to watch. Not with post_url.

max_matches.description: Lifetime cap on signals delivered, and so on credits spent (1-10000). Omit for no cap.

tools.name: update_monitor
tools.description: Change a monitor's settings. Pass only what changes: whatever you omit keeps its current value. The type, post_url and profile_url cannot be changed — delete the monitor and create a new one instead. A list or icp_filters you pass replaces the current one entirely (keywords: ["a"] drops every other keyword); pass an empty one to clear it where the monitor type allows. max_matches, ai_relevance_prompt and lead_list_id are cleared with null. Lowering max_matches below the current match_count pauses the monitor. Changing filters changes the credits charged per signal (see `create_monitor`). Consumes no credits by itself.

keywords.description: Keywords to watch for (max 5, each max 100 characters). Required for keyword_mention, and for post_engagement without post_url or profile_url.

engagement_types.description: post_engagement only (required there): which engagements to catch

target_companies.description: new_hire and job_change only: company names or domains to watch (max 100). Without it, icp_filters is required.

job_offer_title_keywords.description: company_hiring only (required there): job offer title keywords, substring match, any of them (max 10)

industries.description: LinkedIn industry names (Industry Codes V2), e.g. ["Biotechnology"]

job_title_keywords.description: Contact job title keywords (max 10). Not for company_hiring.

icp_filters.description: Narrow the matches to an ideal customer profile. Company-level filters (industries, sizes, countries) and contact-level ones (job titles, seniority) each add 1 credit per signal on keyword_mention and post_engagement.

enrichment_level.description: What to look up for each matched contact. Must be "none" for company_hiring.

lead_list_id.description: Contact list to save every matched contact into, from `list_contact_lists`; null stops saving matches to a list

webhook_url.description: HTTPS URL to notify on each new signal

ai_relevance_prompt.description: What makes a signal relevant to the user (max 500 characters); each signal then gets a 0-5 relevance score; null removes the scoring

is_shared.description: Share the monitor with your current team

max_matches.description: Lifetime cap on signals delivered (1-10000); null removes the cap

tools.name: delete_monitor
tools.description: Delete a signal monitor: it stops watching and stops charging credits at once. This is irreversible — neither the API nor these tools can restore it, for you or for teammates it was shared with; recreating it starts a new monitor from zero. Signals are only readable through a monitor that still exists, so the ones only this monitor caught disappear from `list_signals` and `get_signal` with it — export what the user wants to keep first. Confirm with the user before calling it. Consumes no credits.
